items.item: Model parameters N (input), M (memory), B (block), plus D disks/P CPUs; cost = number of block transfers, in-memory compute treated as free
Scan bound Θ(N/B): reading N items costs N/B transfers, so bytes per transfer, not item count, set the price
Sort bound Θ((N/B)·log_{M/B}(N/B)), tight with constant ≈2; for realistic B the hard part is routing data, not comparing it
Permuting bound Θ(min(N, Sort(N))): just moving items to target positions is as hard as sorting; many O(N)-in-RAM problems are nonlinear in I/O
Search bound Θ(log_B N) plus Output Θ(Z/B): why B-trees beat binary search (log2 of N/B) on disk
log_{M/B}(N/B) is a small constant (≈2–3) in practice, so external sort ≈ a few read+write passes; keep the log visible because constants matter
Why CPU big-O misleads: an O(N) algorithm with random access (out-of-core hashing, pointer chasing) costs ~N I/Os, B times a scan, and loses to an O(N log N) sort-based one

Index-vs-scan crossover: unclustered lookup of k rows ≈ k random page reads (+ log_B N), full scan ≈ N/B sequential; break-even selectivity ≈ (seq/random cost ratio)/(rows per page), usually well under a few percent
